story:
Can I train a fly-brain model to pass Germany’s citizenship test before me?

This started with a message from a friend: a fly passing the Einbürgerungstest before me would have potential.

A tiny nervous system. German bureaucracy. A very reasonable research agenda.

Google, HHMI Janelia and collaborators had released a detailed reconstruction of the male fruit fly’s central nervous system. The obvious temptation was to put a glowing brain next to a test and make the score go up.

I wanted the answers to come from a computational model constrained by the released fly wiring. So we built an experiment, kept the failed runs, and asked a smaller question first: can this particular model learn a simple association?

The first result is now in. It learned four directly stimulated neural signals. It has not passed the citizenship test.

WHAT THE GOOGLE RESEARCH ACTUALLY GIVES US

The male-CNS project reports more than 166,000 neurons and roughly 125 million synaptic connections across the brain and ventral nerve cord. The anatomy supports investigations of cell types, sensory routes, movement pathways and differences between male and female circuits.

A structural map does not supply a complete working brain. It does not uniquely determine membrane dynamics, physiological connection strengths, a sensory interface or a learning rule.

Our retained graph has 166,700 neurons, 25,582,938 directed cell-to-cell edges and 124,177,617 aggregated contacts. We use that released connectivity. The simulation’s leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics and learning parameters are additional, explicit assumptions. This is an independent experiment, not a Google result or endorsement.

THE FIRST ATTEMPT FAILED BEFORE GERMAN

Before questions, the model received a simpler visual task: identify which of four quadrants contained a bright patch.

The designated memory and answer populations stayed silent. The learning rule changed no candidate weights. Held-out performance was 0/16.

We preserved that result. A separate, untrained 33-question practice sitting also scored 0/33, with every answer abstained.

The next audit logged 110 calibration trials across 22 configurations. We examined retinal drive, memory excitability, visual coverage, anatomically connected outputs and relay currents. No configuration met the declared visual admission criteria.

The audit exposed concrete problems: uneven coverage in our retinal projection, and two initially selected answer populations without direct input from the chosen visual Kenyon-cell subtype. Correcting these design choices did not establish visual learning.

ISOLATING THE LEARNING MECHANISM

To separate the learning rule from that sensory obstacle, we declared a direct-stimulation positive control.

We selected four disjoint groups of 16 visual Kenyon cells. Each trial directly stimulated one group. No image or German question entered this control.

Across 128 training presentations, a supervised local rule changed only existing connections from Kenyon cells to designated mushroom-body output populations. The graph topology stayed fixed. The four output populations had fixed A–D labels.

There was no language model, OCR, embedding model or external learned classifier making the choice. During training, target labels entered the weight update. During frozen evaluation, the stimulus alone drove the model, and its output firing rates determined the choice.

THE RESULT, INCLUDING THE CONTROLS

For the first neural-ensemble set, frozen evaluation produced:

• Untrained: 9/32 lab trials correct.
• Trained: 32/32.
• Shuffled training labels: 8/32.
• Existing connection weights changed: 178.

A replication used different neural ensembles and fresh seeds:

• Untrained: 8/32 lab trials correct.
• Trained: 30/32.
• Shuffled training labels: 0/32.
• Existing connection weights changed: 244.

These evaluations used fresh stimulation strengths for four familiar neural patterns. They did not test unseen visual categories or German comprehension.

Reloading the first saved checkpoint reproduced every evaluated total spike count, output rate and choice. Resetting its learned weights dropped it back to 9/32. Silencing Kenyon cells yielded 0/32.

That is useful evidence that learning within this custom neural model changed its behavior. It is not biological validation, and it does not show that the measured fly anatomy was necessary: a matched topology control remains a further experiment.

HOW LONG UNTIL IT PASSES?

The official citizenship test has 33 questions, with 17 correct required to pass. The 32-trial numbers above belong only to our separate lab control.

Each control training run contained 51.2 simulated seconds. Compute time on this sparse, directly stimulated workload cannot be extrapolated into a time-to-pass estimate for visual questions. We have not measured a citizenship learning curve, so there is no defensible answer in minutes, hours or days yet.

Next comes a functioning sensory route, calibrated against biological visual-response evidence. Then the model must pass the fixed visual-learning task with frozen evaluation and controls. Only after that does citizenship training start.

Even success on a familiar public question bank would leave a harder question: did it recognize the questions, or learn concepts that generalize to new German wording?

That is the journey I want to document. The little fly has learned something. German bureaucracy is still ahead.
